en: Making a spectacle, upon those dogs
He will take my revenge for me.'
Saying this, your mother,
Running, unable to restrain herself,
Her heart trembling,
Your mother rejoiced beyond measure.
To your mother the earth spun in a haze.
Paying the doe no heed,
Your mother came in,
Drawing near to her orphan then.
As your mother rushed up,
That doe was a spirit:
It hurried away, did you see?
No eye could catch it,
No one could tell where it was—
It fled away, did you see?
When your mother came in,
She had committed a fault.
No eye could catch it,
No one could tell where it was.
That white doe standing there
Had vanished into the unseen.
In wonderful delight,
Semetey was immersed.
Mist and vapor rose from his head;
There Semetey lay.
A spirit had settled upon him, imposing;
Semetey remained there.
Having drunk deeply of the spirit's milk.
Semetey had drunk it.
In great delight
Semetey had reveled;
Sweating profusely, giving off steam,
Semetey lay there.
Look at the child one way:
He had a dragon's appearance.
Look at the child another way:
He had the majesty of six thousand warriors.
At that rocky spring in the valley,
Without the slightest fear of his majesty,
She found her little one after mortal anguish.
At that spring among rocky cliffs,
After suffering, Kanykei found
The little one left by the mighty warrior.
Your mother, blessed by Kydyr, was a noble lion.
That was where she found her child!
The voice of your fierce mother
Had reached God.
Life was sweet; she did not die,
But over the only child she had found after mortal anguish
She flung herself then.
Clasping the child to her breast,
Your mother rejoiced,
Took her kerchief in her hand,
And to Allah, the one God,
Vowed a horse with crescent hooves;
To her peerless lion Manas
She vowed a camel with two humps.
The gray belt-pouch left by Manas—
Had it not descended from heaven?
That pouch, companion to the Magnanimous One,
She fitted closely round her neck,
For her companion in the wilderness
Praying to the one God.
Semetey had taken the doe's milk
And drunk more than his fill.
The milk his belly could not hold
Poured from both corners of his mouth;
Six leather pails of white curds
Quivered on either side
And set upon the ground.
Your peerless mother Kanykei,
Overflowing with gratitude to God,
Put them in her kerchief.
Her orphan in her right arm,
Those curds left as a gift
Your valiant mother Kanykei
Wrapped securely in her kerchief.
Praying earnestly to God,
With her orphan and the curds,
Kanykei hurried along
And brought them to her mother.
Her fair face toward the direction of prayer
Chyiyrdy had turned;
Praying to God,
Chyiyrdy was standing there.
When she saw Chyiyrdy,
Kanykei could not contain herself:
“O my cherished, sacred mother,
My mother, great as a mountain!
Your soft little gray-and-white falcon—
My dear mother, here he is,
Your gray goshawk, your morning star!
My cherished mother,
Your words proved true.
This child crawling away from his cradle—
Mother, it was Allah's mysterious doing.
A spirit suckled your child:
The words you spoke proved true.
Mother, drink and set your heart at rest:
This is the spirit's milk.
Give your blessing to the only child
And break the power of all your grief.
My sacred mother before me,
From the Kyrgyz who had their king,
Mounted on my broad back,
My widowhood made plain,
You are the mother I brought away!
Mother, God has granted your wish.
To the only child left by your son,
The golden-antlered white doe,
Mother, gave her teat while chewing her cud.
The white curds left over from your child's mouth,
Thinking, ‘Let my grieving mother drink,’
Your daughter-in-law has brought.
Grieve no more, mother; raise your head:
She has come and given them to you!”
Then Chyiyrdy
The white curds her daughter-in-law had given,
They shared, drank and had their fill;
Their burning grief subsided,
All the sorrow in their breasts relaxed,
Their eyes, small as dough pellets, opened.
The two ladies fervently uttered wishes;
The lost orphan had been found,
And the fleeing widows
Had their honor preserved by this.
Taking the child as their support,
The two ladies greatly cheered their hearts.
Then your aged mother Chyiyrdy said:
“O my cherished Kanykei,
Do not weep, my foal.
Grief cannot make amends;
One who keeps lamenting will not prosper.
O Kanykei, my foal,
Give no more thought to sorrow.
Let us take comfort
In this child left by Manas.
Let us live and not die,
O Kanykei, my foal;
Let us care for your orphan for twelve years.
This Semetey here
Will be a lion upheld by the holy patron.
If my orphan survives,
He will be a hero like his father.
My Manas, gone to the Last Judgment,
Was dear to the Kyrgyz.
A true heir has remained behind him;
He was the child left as seed from my Manas.
The black-spotted leopard,
Bounding at his side,
Has surely taken this child of mine
Under its unseen protection.
My Manas, gone to the true world,
Has surely kept watch over him.
The short-tailed, gray-maned lion
Of Manas, gone to the other world,
Was the manifest companion.
Thinking, ‘My orphan has set out on a distant journey,’
He must have watched him without wavering.
The patrons who protected my Manas
Must have carried my orphan away.
The forty Chiltens, Kydyr and Ilyas,
Changing into a doe,
Must have given my child their teat.
The patrons who accompanied my Manas
Must all have come together to this orphan.
O Kanykei, by Baabedin,
My foal, God has granted your wish!
O Kanykei, my foal,
If your orphan lives long,
His right shoulder will be broad,
His twelve limbs well proportioned.
Like Manas, gone to the other world,
This child will be a lion like his father.
He will be a blaze of glowing embers;
The enemy he charges will be stopped.
He will set grassy land afire.
If he survives, Semetey
Will kindle the feather-grass plains,
Will pour blood into the running water.
When he returns, he will lead a migration.
Put aside your grief, Kanykei.
When he returns to Talas,
You will see him avenge himself on the six villains!
If God lets him see the Kyrgyz,
O Kanykei, my foal,
He will fulfill your wish.
When he grows enraged,
He will have men's heads cut off.
Those who understand his words
He will bring to obedience by words;
To a fool who will not understand,
He will show that he is a lion.
When his anger is roused,
He will chase white deer and make them cattle.
If my orphan takes after his father,
He will throw the whole world into turmoil.
This orphan left you by the gray-maned hero
Will herd gray deer and make them cattle.
If he grows safely without dying,
He will throw every land he sees into turmoil.
O Kanykei, do not grieve:
God has granted your wish.
Manas, gone to the Last Judgment,
Had a dervish companion.
As I lay at night, I saw
He had come to your child's cradle.
Saying, ‘The orphan left by Manas,’
He had offered your orphan his hand.
The one clasping his hand
Was the naked old man Kydyr.
To tell the child
He had words of counsel.
Standing there that night, the dervish
Said this to Semetey:
‘Do not shrink from an enemy exchanging shots.
Death is in God's hands;
Do not retreat from an enemy you meet.
Until you reach twelve,
You will be in the city of Bukhara.
When your age reaches twelve,
You will return to your village.
May all your fortunes prosper;
My foal, become a greater lion than your father!’
The dervish gave his blessing;
I saw him set things right.
That gray-maned king Manas—
I saw how he protected him.
I saw Baabedin of the road
Grant the orphan passage.
All the lions blessed by Kydyr,
Raising a shout,
I saw grant the orphan passage.
Calling him the pennant fastened to the spear,
To your father Temir's city
Let us wander, carrying him on our backs.
Calling him the gift left by the Magnanimous One,
The hoof left by the winged steed,
Let us present him as a fitting gift,
The lamp left by the falcon.
O Kanykei, my foal,
Grieving is of no use:
Your gray-maned Manas will not return.
Lamenting offers no remedy;
What is seen today is gone tomorrow.
O Kanykei, my foal,
Such is this shitty world!
Put aside your pride and shame,
O Kanykei, my foal:
Your magnanimous Manas is not here!
Traveling forty days without rest,
My child, let us settle as wanderers in Bukhara.
Until your orphan reaches twelve,
Do not cling to pride without cause.
Let us bear the name of wanderers!
